entries.summary: Introduced on November 23, 2026 under Premier Danielle Smith as a 163-page First Reading omnibus bill (168-page PDF amending 20 provincial statutes), Section 12 of Bill 44 repeals the Police Act's 2025 Crown-corporation structure (s. 33.4(2)) and the Bill 15 employee-transfer chapters (Parts 3.3 and 3.4). It establishes the Alberta Sheriffs Police Service directly as a non-corporate statutory force whose employees are appointed under the Public Service Act, shifts municipal service contracts under s. 33.75 to the Crown in right of Alberta, and provides a three-year transitional wind-down window for the existing corporation (s. 33.951).
entries.title: Bill 44 repeals the Alberta Sheriffs Police Service's Crown-corporation status and moves staff under the Public Service Act

entries.summary: Section 6 of Bill 44 repeals Fatality Inquiries Act s. 33(3)—codified in 2005 (PC era) and narrowed in 2017 (Notley NDP, SA 2017 c 8 s 2) only to carve out youth deaths already reviewed by the Child and Youth Advocate (s. 33(3.1)-(3.2)) while keeping adult peace-officer and correctional custody inquiries mandatory unless due solely to natural, unpreventable causes or unrelated to care. In its place, the Board applies unpublished Cabinet-prescribed factors (ss. 33(2), 55(e)) with no statutory duty to publish reasons when declining an inquiry. Section 6 also downgrades next-of-kin medical-examiner report access to discretionary under regulation (s. 30(2)), adds compulsory addiction facilities to medical-examiner notification only (s. 12(1)(a)), and contains no transitional savings clause for pending inquiries.
entries.title: Bill 44 repeals mandatory public fatality inquiries for custodial deaths, shifts next-of-kin report access to regulation, and omits a transitional clause

entries.summary: Verified primary statutes across four Canadian provinces distinguish policing structure from custodial-death inquests. On policing, Ontario's Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019 (s. 2(1)) employs OPP officers under Ontario's Public Service Act and Quebec's Police Act (s. 50) places the Sûreté du Québec under the Minister of Public Security—both non-corporate ministry models. On custodial deaths, however, British Columbia (Coroners Act, s. 18(2)-(2.1)), Manitoba (The Fatality Inquiries Act, s. 19(5)), and Ontario (Coroners Act, s. 10(4)) all mandate public inquests for custodial or peace-officer force deaths (with BC obligating published reasons whenever waived), whereas Quebec pairs discretionary inquests (Coroners Act, ss. 104-106) with mandatory independent BEI police-death investigations (Police Act, ss. 289.1-289.2).
entries.title: Four-province statutory baseline: ON and QC house police under ministries, while BC, MB, and ON mandate custodial inquests

entries.summary: In December 2025, the government-appointed Alberta Next Panel recommended transitioning community policing from the RCMP to an Alberta Police Service prior to the 2032 contract expiry without holding a referendum—arguing that over 80% of Albertans already receive policing from municipal services or Alberta Sheriffs—even though its own report recorded 52% opposition in professional polling (44%, 41%, and 48% support across three 2025 waves, lowest of seven measures) and majority opposition in online surveys. Cabinet's Orders in Council 109/2026, 110/2026, and 160/2026 set ten questions for the October 19, 2026 stand-alone referendum with zero questions on RCMP replacement.
entries.title: Alberta Next Panel advised against a policing referendum despite 52% polling opposition, and the October 19, 2026 ballot omitted RCMP replacement

entries.summary: Two distinct non-summable financial baselines frame Alberta's policing debate. Under Premier Jason Kenney, the October 2021 PwC Transition Study forecast roughly $366M over six years in transition costs (about $241M operating and $125M capital) and $735M to $759M in annual operating costs for a full provincial police force, alongside roughly $170M per year in federal RCMP cost-sharing (30% under PPSA; 30% or 10% under MPSAs). Separately, under Premier Danielle Smith, the Renewed Police Funding Model effective April 1, 2026 increases rural and small-municipality shares of actual frontline PPSA costs from 22% in 2026-27 by two percentage points annually to 30% in 2030-31+, while adding a Vacancy Modifier and Population Density Subsidy.
entries.title: Separate bases: 2021 PwC forecast (~$366M transition, $735M-$759M/yr) vs. 2026-2031 municipal cost-share ramp (22% to 30%)

pages.summary: Separate-basis financial reconciliation of Alberta Sheriffs and Contract Policing Estimates, the 2021 PwC forecast, the 2026-2031 Police Funding Model ramp, the Alberta Next Panel report, and ministerial accounts.
pages.title: Policing Budgets, Municipal Cost-Sharing & Referendum Mandate

scopes.coverage: Public-record slice of Alberta's 2019–23 DynaLIFE community laboratory contract from the November 2025 Auditor General examination, AHS audited FY 2022–23 and 2023–24 financial statements, January 27, 2022 public AHS board minutes, November 20, 2025 Alberta Hansard, March 18, 2026 Main Estimates, November 2026 OAG recommendation status summaries, November 17, 2026 Public Accounts Committee testimony, and a reconciliation note on November 19, 2025 Global News / Canadian Press $109M headline reporting. Former-vendor operational claims remain privately held pending outreach.

Primary-record audit of Alberta Bill 44 (163-page First Reading bill / 168-page PDF amending 20 statutes, Nov. 23, 2026), OIC 241/2025 & OIC 116/2026, 2005-2026 policing/inquiry/detention statutes (PC, NDP, Kenney & Smith eras), 2025-27 Government Estimates, 2021 PwC APPS Transition Study, Renewed Police Funding Model, Alberta Next Panel Report, Oct. 19, 2026 referendum OICs, and ON/QC/BC/MB primary statutory baselines. Active criminal proceedings and unretrieved stakeholder submissions remain privately excluded.

images.alt: Dark charcoal editorial magazine cover titled Inside Alberta's Bill 44 Overhaul — File #02: Direct ministry police. Custody inquiries rewritten. $200.9M budget. Illustration shows a crown-stamped brass padlock clamping shut a leather courtroom inquiry ledger and a 7-point sheriff's star badge on a ministerial desk beside red-ribboned legislative binders and a wooden ballot box taped shut.
images.label: Cover: Inside Alberta's Bill 44 Overhaul (File #02)

images.alt: Editorial comic panel 1 of 4 titled Step 1: Dissolve the Firewall. A smiling official in a navy suit uses giant brass shears to cut down a glowing teal partition between a ministerial desk with an upright brass shield and a sheriff's dispatch console with a Stetson hat and microphone. Caption cites Bill 49 (2025), OIC 116/2026, and Bill 44 repealing corporate status while retaining Police Act s. 33.94(2) operational non-interference.
images.label: Panel 1/4: Step 1 — Dissolve the Firewall

images.alt: Editorial comic panel 2 of 4 titled Step 2: Rewrite Custody Inquiries. Bureaucrats pull heavy crimson velvet curtains shut across an open courtroom doorway in front of waiting citizens while an official locks red-wax-sealed scrolls inside a brass cabinet. Caption compares existing Fatality Inquiries Act s. 33(3) and BC's Coroners Act s. 18 with Bill 44 repealing mandatory custody inquiries in favour of unpublished Cabinet regulations with no s. 6 transitional clause.
images.label: Panel 2/4: Step 2 — Rewrite Custody Inquiries

images.alt: Editorial comic panel 3 of 4 titled Step 3: Skip Ballot, Ramp the Tab. At a rural prairie municipal counter with a grain elevator outside, a startled councillor faces towering ledger folders and gold coin stacks while an official wheels a chained ballot box out a side door. Caption notes 52% polling opposition in the Alberta Next Panel report, omission from all 10 Oct. 2026 ballot questions, $200.942M Sheriffs budget, and 22% to 30% rural cost-share ramp.
images.label: Panel 3/4: Step 3 — Skip Ballot, Ramp the Tab

images.alt: Editorial comic panel 4 of 4 titled Step 4: Link Health Data, No Consent. Glowing teal tubes siphon medical-cross folders out of hospital filing cabinets into a dark central server tower while a puzzled patient holds a blank unsigned clipboard. Caption summarizes Bill 44 Section 10 non-consensual health data disclosure, binding disclosure orders, and Cabinet HIA overrides alongside OIPC privacy filings and Ministers' Hansard rationale.
images.label: Panel 4/4: Step 4 — Link Health Data, No Consent

share_kits.summary: Download the 5 verified 1080×1080 satirical comic panels and copy the ready-to-post Facebook caption and First Comment backed by 23 primary statutory and budget records.
share_kits.title: Share Bill 44 on Facebook — 5-Panel Comic Kit (File #02)

images.alt: Dark charcoal editorial magazine cover titled Alberta's DynaLIFE Playbook — File #01: No documented business case. One bidder. A $31.5M buyback. Satirical illustration shows a brass seesaw on a glowing teal medical-cross fulcrum slammed down by chained, redacted, crimson-bowed contract folders with a cracked smoking piggy bank, launching a rack of blood-sample test tubes and a crumpled napkin into the air.
images.label: Cover: Alberta's DynaLIFE Playbook (File #01)

images.alt: Editorial comic panel 1 of 4 titled Step 1: Skip the Homework. A smiling cartoon official throws blank pages out a boardroom window while pointing to a crumpled napkin as a stunned analyst searches the empty table with a magnifying glass. Caption notes the Auditor General found no documented formal business case from AHS or Alberta Health before procurement began.
images.label: Panel 1/4: Step 1 — Skip the Homework

images.alt: Editorial comic panel 2 of 4 titled Step 2: The One-Bidder Auction. A rival bidder dashes out an exit door with a suitcase while one lone corporate bidder lounges with feet up holding an auction paddle as an auctioneer bangs a gavel beside a tray of glass lab test tubes. Caption notes Sonic Healthcare exited over pandemic travel curbs, leaving one bidder for a $4.8B prospective commitment.
images.label: Panel 2/4: Step 2 — The One-Bidder Auction

images.alt: Editorial comic panel 3 of 4 titled Step 3: Pay to Buy It Back. An exhausted health official hands a giant ribboned envelope across a counter for a wooden crate of lab test tubes while a tipped piggy bank smokes behind him. Caption separates the Auditor General's $77M extra-cost estimate from AHS's $31.5M buyout cash paid.
images.label: Panel 3/4: Step 3 — Pay to Buy It Back

images.alt: Editorial comic panel 4 of 4 titled Step 4: Full Cooperation. A bewildered auditor examines a chained, redacted filing cabinet with a magnifying glass while a cheerful official gives a thumbs-up leaning on a broom beside a lumpy rug hiding folders. Caption cites the Auditor General's restricted-access finding alongside Premier Smith's Hansard statement that the government cooperated fully.
images.label: Panel 4/4: Step 4 — Full Cooperation
